column2: walking on a path in a big park with your family
column3: stay where your grown-up can see you and agree on a meeting place, such as a bench or the gate, in case you get separated
column4: parks are big and crowded, and a meeting place helps you find each other quickly

column2: seeing a sign that says «keep off the grass»
column3: walk on the paths and not on the grass
column4: the grass may be newly seeded or resting, and the park keepers want it to grow

column2: feeding bread to ducks at the pond
column3: give ducks only small amounts of duck food, peas or oats, or nothing at all, and never bread
column4: bread fills ducks up without feeding them, makes them sick and dirties the water

column2: a squirrel comes close and seems to want food
column3: do not feed or touch it; watch it from a distance
column4: wild animals can bite or scratch, and food from people is bad for them

column2: finding a park bench wet with fresh paint
column3: read the «wet paint» sign and choose another bench
column4: the paint will stick to your clothes and the bench will be spoiled

column2: a dog off its lead runs towards you in the park
column3: stand still like a tree, arms by your sides, do not run or scream, and let the owner call it
column4: running makes a dog chase you; standing still usually makes it lose interest

column2: wanting to pat a stranger's dog in the park
column3: ask the owner first, then let the dog sniff your hand before you stroke its side
column4: not every dog is friendly with children, and the owner knows best

column2: public toilets in the park
column3: go with your grown-up or tell them where you are going, and wash your hands after
column4: public places can be unsafe for a child alone, and hands carry germs

column2: the park is getting dark in the evening
column3: go home before dark or stay with your grown-up
column4: in the dark it is harder to see dangers and harder for others to see you

column2: flying a kite in the park
column3: fly it in an open space far from power lines, trees and roads, and never in a storm
column4: a kite caught on a power line can give a deadly electric shock

column2: a kite gets stuck on a power line
column3: let go of the string at once, do not pull it, and tell a grown-up to call the power company
column4: electricity can travel down a wet or metallic string into your body

column2: riding a bike or scooter on a shared park path
column3: ride slowly, keep to one side, ring your bell and give way to people walking
column4: walkers, small children and dogs can step in front of you without warning

column2: the slide is hot after sitting in the summer sun
column3: touch it with your hand before sliding down
column4: metal and plastic in strong sun can burn your skin

column2: climbing up the slide while others slide down
column3: go up the ladder and down the slide, one at a time
column4: you can crash into a child coming down and both get hurt

column2: walking in front of the swings
column3: walk around the swings, well away from the front and back
column4: a moving swing hits hard and can knock you over

column2: standing up or twisting on a swing
column3: sit in the middle of the seat, hold on with both hands and stop the swing before getting off
column4: jumping off or standing up is a common cause of broken arms

column2: wearing a scarf or a hood with cords on the climbing frame
column3: take off scarves, bike helmets and anything with cords before playing
column4: cords and scarves can catch on equipment and strangle a child

column2: a younger child is waiting for a turn on the swing
column3: share and take turns, for example ten swings each
column4: taking turns is fair and everyone has fun

column2: finding broken glass or a needle in the sandpit
column3: do not touch it; move away and tell a grown-up
column4: glass cuts and a used needle can carry dangerous illnesses

column2: a playground after rain
column3: check that the equipment is not slippery before climbing
column4: wet metal and plastic are slippery and you can fall

column2: a child falls from the climbing frame and does not get up
column3: do not move them; stay close and call a grown-up at once
column4: moving someone with a hurt neck or back can make it worse

column2: a friend dares you to jump from the top of the climbing frame
column3: say no and climb down
column4: a high jump onto hard ground can break bones

column2: the playground is frozen or icy in winter
column3: keep off the equipment that is covered in ice
column4: ice makes surfaces very slippery and falls on ice are hard

column2: licking a metal pole in freezing weather
column3: never put your tongue or lips on frozen metal; if stuck, ask for lukewarm (not hot) water to be poured on
column4: your wet tongue freezes to the metal and tears when you pull it away

column2: helping to plant seeds in the garden
column3: plant at the depth on the packet, water gently and label the row
column4: seeds need the right depth, water and light to sprout

column2: watering plants on a hot summer day
column3: water in the early morning or evening, at the roots
column4: in the heat of midday much of the water evaporates

column2: picking flowers in someone else's garden or a public park
column3: only pick flowers in your own garden or with permission
column4: the flowers belong to someone and are there for everyone to enjoy

column2: finding a worm on the garden path
column3: pick it up gently with wet hands and put it back on the soil
column4: worms dry out on paths, and they keep soil healthy

column2: using garden tools such as a rake or shears
column3: use them only with a grown-up, lay a rake with the teeth down, and carry shears closed and pointing down
column4: sharp tools and an upturned rake cause bad cuts and injuries

column2: a grown-up is mowing the lawn
column3: stay indoors or far away and never ride on or go near a running mower
column4: mowers throw stones and their blades cut off fingers and toes

column2: a bottle of weed killer or slug pellets in the shed
column3: never touch, open or taste garden chemicals
column4: they are poisons that can make people and pets very ill

column2: a lovely bright berry on a garden bush
column3: never eat any berry, seed or leaf unless a grown-up says it is safe
column4: many garden plants, such as yew, foxglove and laburnum, are poisonous

column2: eating a tomato or strawberry straight from the garden
column3: wash it first and ask a grown-up
column4: soil, animal droppings and sprays may be on it

column2: a bee buzzing around the flowers
column3: keep calm and move away slowly; do not swat it
column4: a bee only stings when it feels threatened, and bees pollinate the flowers

column2: the pond in the garden
column3: never play near a pond alone, and young children must always be watched
column4: a small child can drown in just a few centimetres of water

column2: a hosepipe on a hot day
column3: ask before playing with it and let the first water run out before spraying people
column4: water left in a hose in the sun can get hot enough to scald

column2: finding a hedgehog in the garden
column3: leave it alone; offer a shallow dish of water, never milk
column4: milk makes hedgehogs ill, and they are wild animals

column2: a bird's nest in a bush
column3: look from a distance and never touch the nest or eggs
column4: the parents may abandon it, and in many places disturbing nests is against the law

column2: digging in the garden soil
column3: wear gloves and wash your hands well afterwards
column4: soil can contain germs and animal droppings

column2: walking in a forest with your family
column3: stay on the marked trail and keep your group in sight
column4: off the trail you can get lost, fall, or damage plants

column2: becoming separated from your group in the woods
column3: stop, stay where you are, hug a tree, and blow a whistle three times or shout
column4: it is easier for searchers to find someone who stays in one place

column2: carrying a whistle on a walk
column3: keep one on a string or in your pocket
column4: a whistle can be heard much further than a voice and does not tire you

column2: a dead tree or a big branch hanging loose
column3: do not stand or play under it, and never shelter under it in wind
column4: dead branches can fall without warning, especially in wind

column2: climbing a tree
column3: climb only low, strong, healthy trees with a grown-up nearby, and test each branch
column4: thin or dead branches snap and falls from trees break bones

column2: finding deer tracks or animal droppings on the path
column3: look closely but do not touch the droppings
column4: tracks tell you which animals live there; droppings carry germs

column2: seeing a deer, fox or other wild animal
column3: stay still and quiet, watch from far away, and never try to feed or touch it
column4: wild animals are frightened by people and can kick or bite

column2: finding a baby bird on the ground
column3: leave it alone unless it is in danger; the parents are usually close by
column4: young birds learn to fly from the ground and the parents still feed them

column2: finding a baby deer or fawn alone
column3: leave it where it is and walk away
column4: the mother hides it and comes back; touching it may make her abandon it

column2: walking in the forest during hunting season
column3: wear bright orange or other bright colours and stay on trails
column4: hunters must be able to see that you are a person

column2: carving your name into a tree
column3: never carve or peel the bark of a tree
column4: the wound lets in disease and can kill the tree

column2: breaking branches off living trees for a den
column3: use only fallen sticks and leave living plants alone
column4: living trees are homes for animals and take years to grow

column2: finding an old well, mine or deep hole in the woods
column3: keep far away and tell a grown-up
column4: the ground near old holes can collapse and you could fall in

column2: getting ready for a hike
column3: wear good shoes, take water, a snack, a hat, a raincoat and tell someone where you are going
column4: weather changes, you get thirsty and hungry, and someone should know your route

column2: feeling tired and thirsty on a long walk
column3: tell your grown-up, rest and drink water
column4: pushing on when exhausted leads to falls and heat sickness

column2: getting a blister on your foot
column3: tell a grown-up early and cover it with a plaster or blister pad
column4: a small rub left alone becomes a painful open sore

column2: coming to a steep cliff edge with a nice view
column3: stay well back from the edge and behind any fence
column4: edges can crumble and a fall can be deadly

column2: crossing a farmer's field with cows
column3: walk calmly around the edge, close gates behind you and keep any dog on a lead
column4: cows protect their calves and can charge, and open gates let animals escape

column2: a gate on a country path
column3: leave every gate as you found it: closed if it was closed, open if it was open
column4: farmers leave gates the way they need them for their animals

column2: the path is blocked by a fallen tree or flooded stream
column3: turn back or find a safe way round with your grown-up
column4: climbing over or wading through can be dangerous

column2: meeting other walkers on a narrow path
column3: step aside, say hello and let them pass, uphill walkers usually go first
column4: it is polite and safe on narrow trails

column2: walking on a country road with no pavement
column3: walk in single file facing the oncoming traffic and wear something bright
column4: you can see cars coming and drivers can see you

column2: using a map or trail signs
column3: learn to read the trail markers and check them at every junction
column4: it keeps you on the right path and helps you find your way back

column2: the sun is going down but you are still far from home
column3: tell your grown-up; carry a torch and always plan to be back before dark
column4: paths are hard to follow and easy to fall on in the dark

column2: walking in the mountains
column3: start early, turn back if the weather gets worse, and stay together
column4: mountain weather changes quickly and storms, cold and fog come fast

column2: walking near the edge of a quarry or old mine
column3: stay away and do not climb or swim there
column4: quarry rocks fall and quarry water is very deep and cold

column2: setting up a tent
column3: pitch it on flat, high ground away from dead trees, rivers and the bottom of slopes
column4: low ground floods in rain and dead trees can fall

column2: going to the toilet at a campsite without toilets
column3: go with a grown-up, at least 60 metres (about 200 feet) from water, and bury it or pack it out
column4: this keeps the water clean and the camp pleasant for others

column2: leaving food in the tent
column3: keep food in sealed boxes, in the car or in a bear box, never in the tent
column4: smells attract animals such as raccoons, possums, foxes and bears

column2: camping in bear country in North America
column3: store food in bear-proof containers, keep a clean camp and stay with adults
column4: bears are attracted by food smells and can be dangerous

column2: using a camping stove or lantern inside the tent
column3: never use a stove, heater or barbecue inside a tent
column4: they can set the tent on fire and give off carbon monoxide, a poison gas you cannot smell

column2: waking up in the night in the tent
column3: take a torch and wake a grown-up before going out
column4: in the dark you can trip, get lost or walk into the fire pit

column2: drinking water from a stream at a campsite
column3: only drink water that has been boiled, filtered or treated
column4: even clear stream water can carry germs that cause bad illness

column2: packing up at the end of a camping trip
column3: pick up every bit of litter and leave the place as you found it
column4: it keeps nature clean for animals and the next campers

column2: tent ropes in the dark
column3: watch where you walk and do not run between tents
column4: tent ropes and pegs trip people up

column2: the night is colder than expected
column3: wear a hat and dry layers to sleep, and sleep on a mat, not straight on the ground
column4: the ground draws heat from your body and a hat keeps your head warm

column2: wanting to make a campfire
column3: only make a fire with a grown-up, in a fire ring or allowed place, and check that fires are permitted
column4: fires spread quickly and many areas ban fires in dry weather

column2: a fire ban is in force
column3: do not light any fire, not even a small one
column4: in dry weather one spark can start a wildfire that burns homes and forests

column2: sitting near the campfire
column3: stay outside a safe circle, about three big steps away, and never run around the fire
column4: you can trip and fall into the fire

column2: roasting marshmallows
column3: use a long stick or fork, hold the marshmallow at the side of the flames and blow it out if it catches fire
column4: burning marshmallow sticks to skin and burns badly

column2: throwing things into the fire
column3: never throw rubbish, plastic, cans, aerosols or glass into a fire
column4: plastic gives poisonous smoke and cans and aerosols can explode

column2: the fire goes out and the ashes look cold
column3: drown the fire with water, stir, and drown again until it is cold to the touch
column4: hidden embers can stay hot for many hours and start a wildfire

column2: your clothes catch fire
column3: stop, drop to the ground, cover your face and roll
column4: running fans the flames; rolling smothers them

column2: getting a small burn from the fire
column3: cool it under cool running water for 20 minutes and tell a grown-up
column4: cooling stops the burn going deeper; ice or butter make it worse

column2: the smoke blows into your face
column3: move to the other side of the fire, away from the wind
column4: smoke hurts eyes and lungs

column2: poking the fire with a stick and waving it around
column3: keep burning sticks in the fire and never wave them
column4: sparks and hot ends can burn people and start fires

column2: playing on the river bank
column3: stay back from the edge, especially after rain
column4: banks can be slippery or crumble into the water

column2: wanting to swim in a river
column3: only swim in places that are known to be safe, with a grown-up watching
column4: rivers have hidden currents, cold water, rocks and snags under the surface

column2: the river looks calm on the surface
column3: remember that the water under the surface can still be moving fast
column4: calm-looking water can pull a swimmer downstream

column2: walking across a river on stepping stones or a log
column3: only cross where there is a bridge or with a grown-up who says it is safe
column4: wet stones and logs are slippery and a fall into a river is dangerous

column2: the river is high and brown after heavy rain
column3: keep well away from it
column4: floodwater is fast, strong and carries logs and rubbish

column2: someone falls into the river
column3: do not jump in; shout for help, call the emergency number, and throw something that floats
column4: many people who jump in to save others drown themselves

column2: throwing stones into a river
column3: throw them only where no one is in the water or on the other side
column4: a stone can hurt someone you did not see

column2: fishing with a grown-up
column3: carry hooks in a box, watch behind you when you cast, and take your line home
column4: hooks catch skin and left line traps birds and animals

column2: finding a bridge over a river
column3: cross on the bridge, not on the railings, and never jump off
column4: jumping from bridges into water can hit rocks or shallow water and cause serious injury

column2: looking for small creatures in a stream
column3: lift stones gently, look and then put them back the way they were
column4: the stones are homes for insects and fish eggs

column2: ice on the lake in winter
column3: never walk or skate on a frozen lake unless a grown-up and the local signs say it is safe
column4: ice that looks thick can be thin and break, especially near streams and edges

column2: someone falls through the ice
column3: do not go onto the ice; shout for help, call the emergency number and reach with a long stick or throw a rope from the shore
column4: the ice that broke under them will break under you too

column2: jumping into a lake on a hot day
column3: check the depth with a grown-up first and go in feet first
column4: hidden rocks and shallow water cause head and neck injuries

column2: the water in a lake feels freezing even in summer
column3: get in slowly, stay near the shore and get out if you start shivering
column4: cold water makes you gasp and tires your muscles fast

column2: going out in a boat or canoe
column3: always wear a life jacket that fits, and stay seated
column4: boats tip over, and a life jacket keeps you afloat even if you are tired or hurt

column2: blue-green scum on a lake
column3: do not swim, and keep dogs out of the water
column4: this algae can be poisonous to people and pets

column2: swimming far out to a raft or island
column3: only swim as far as you can easily swim back, with a grown-up watching
column4: distance in water is hard to judge and swimmers get tired

column2: arriving at the beach
column3: swim only between the red and yellow flags where there are lifeguards
column4: lifeguards watch that area and it has been checked for dangers

column2: a red flag is flying at the beach
column3: do not go into the water at all
column4: a red flag means the sea is too dangerous for swimming

column2: being pulled out to sea by a rip current
column3: stay calm, float or swim sideways along the beach, and raise an arm and shout for help
column4: fighting the current tires you out; rips are narrow and you can escape sideways

column2: spotting a rip current
column3: look for a calm-looking dark gap between breaking waves, sometimes with foam or sand drifting out
column4: rips look calm and that is why people choose to swim there

column2: building a deep hole or tunnel in the sand
column3: keep holes no deeper than your knees and never tunnel
column4: sand holes can collapse and bury a person

column2: the tide is coming in
column3: know the tide times and do not walk around cliffs or out to rocks or sandbanks
column4: the rising sea can cut you off with no way back

column2: sitting under a cliff on the beach
column3: stay away from the bottom and the top of cliffs
column4: rocks and soil fall from cliffs without warning

column2: playing on rocks by the sea
column3: keep away from the edge of rocks where waves break
column4: a big wave can knock you into the sea

column2: finding a jellyfish washed up on the sand
column3: do not touch it, even if it looks dead
column4: dead jellyfish can still sting

column2: stung by a jellyfish
column3: get out of the water, tell a lifeguard, and follow local first aid (often rinsing with sea water or vinegar, depending on the region)
column4: treatment differs by type; in Australia some jellyfish are very dangerous

column2: treading on a weever fish or stingray in shallow water
column3: shuffle your feet in shallow water and wear water shoes; put a stung foot in hot (not scalding) water and get help
column4: shuffling warns them away; heat eases the pain of the venom

column2: a crocodile warning sign in northern Australia
column3: never swim in the sea, rivers or lakes where crocodiles may live, and keep away from the water's edge
column4: saltwater crocodiles attack people and hide under the surface

column2: a shark sighting is reported
column3: get out of the water and follow the lifeguards' instructions
column4: lifeguards close beaches to keep people safe

column2: picking up a shell with something living inside
column3: put it back where you found it
column4: shells are homes for living animals

column2: finding a rock pool with crabs and starfish
column3: look gently, hold creatures carefully if allowed, and put them back in the water
column4: they can die out of water and need their homes

column2: finding a cone shell or blue-ringed octopus in an Australian rock pool
column3: never pick them up
column4: they are small and pretty but their venom can kill

column2: finding a strange object washed up on the beach
column3: do not touch metal objects, drums or anything that looks like a bomb or flare; tell a grown-up or lifeguard
column4: old explosives and chemical containers do wash up on shores

column2: a seal or sea lion on the beach
column3: keep far away and keep dogs on a lead
column4: they may look sleepy but can bite and are resting

column2: hot sand on a summer day
column3: wear sandals or beach shoes
column4: dry sand in strong sun can burn the soles of your feet

column2: leaving the beach at the end of the day
column3: take all your litter home, including bottle caps and small bits of plastic
column4: plastic in the sea kills turtles, birds and fish

column2: an inflatable toy drifts out to sea
column3: let it go and tell a grown-up; never swim after it
column4: offshore wind carries inflatables out quickly and swimmers get into trouble chasing them

column2: using a body board or inflatable ring
column3: use them only between the flags and only close to shore
column4: wind and current can carry you away on them

column2: seeing a lifeguard wave at you
column3: look and do what they signal, such as come closer to the shore
column4: lifeguards see dangers you cannot see

column2: the sea suddenly pulls back far from the shore after an earthquake
column3: run to high ground or far inland at once, and do not wait for a warning
column4: this is a sign that a tsunami is coming

column2: swimming in the sea for the first time
column3: stay in shallow water close to a grown-up and do not go out of your depth
column4: waves can knock you over and the sea floor can drop suddenly

column2: big waves coming towards you
column3: turn sideways or dive under the wave with a grown-up near; do not turn your back on the sea
column4: waves can knock you down and roll you along the bottom

column2: swallowing sea water
column3: try not to swallow it and do not drink it
column4: salty water makes you thirstier and can make you sick

column2: someone is in trouble in the water
column3: shout for help, call the lifeguard or emergency number, and throw something that floats; do not swim to them
column4: a panicking swimmer can pull a rescuer under

column2: going on a boat trip
column3: wear a life jacket and stay in the area the crew tells you
column4: people can fall overboard, especially on a moving boat

column2: getting cold in the sea
column3: come out as soon as you start to shiver and dry and dress warmly
column4: cold water takes away body heat fast and causes hypothermia

column2: arriving at a swimming pool
column3: read the pool rules, find the shallow and deep ends, and listen to the lifeguard
column4: knowing where the deep water is keeps non-swimmers safe

column2: running around the edge of the pool
column3: walk, never run
column4: the wet floor is slippery and falls onto hard tiles cause head injuries

column2: diving into the shallow end
column3: only dive where signs say diving is allowed and the water is deep enough
column4: diving into shallow water can break your neck

column2: pushing a friend into the pool or holding them under
column3: never push, dunk or hold anyone under water, even in fun
column4: people can hit the side, swallow water and drown

column2: wanting to go into the deep end
column3: only go when you can swim confidently and a grown-up says yes
column4: tired or weak swimmers can drown quickly in deep water

column2: the pool drain or filter outlet
column3: keep hair, fingers and toys away from drains and outlets
column4: strong suction can hold you under water

column2: needing the toilet while swimming
column3: get out and go to the toilet; shower before getting back in
column4: it keeps the water clean for everyone

column2: a garden or holiday pool with no adult around
column3: never go in or near a pool without a grown-up watching
column4: most child drownings happen in home pools when no one is watching

column2: the pool gate is left open
column3: close it and tell a grown-up
column4: pool fences keep small children from falling in

column2: water wings or a float
column3: know that they are not life-saving equipment and still stay near a grown-up
column4: they can slip off or deflate

column2: spending all afternoon at an outdoor pool
column3: put on sunscreen again after swimming and drink water
column4: water washes sunscreen off and you lose water in the heat even when wet

column2: feeling very tired or cold in the pool
column3: get out, rest and warm up
column4: tiredness and cold make swimming dangerous

column2: playing in the snow
column3: wear a hat, gloves, warm socks and waterproof boots and come in when you get wet or very cold
column4: wet clothes lose heat fast and fingers and toes can get frostbite

column2: fingers turn white and numb in the cold
column3: go indoors and warm them slowly against your body or in lukewarm water, not hot
column4: frostbitten skin can be damaged further by fast heating or rubbing

column2: shivering hard and feeling clumsy and sleepy in the cold
column3: tell a grown-up at once and get warm and dry
column4: these are signs of hypothermia, which is dangerous

column2: sledging down a hill
column3: choose a hill away from roads, trees, fences and water, sit feet first, and use a helmet
column4: collisions with trees and cars cause serious injuries

column2: walking up the sledging hill
column3: walk up at the side, not in the middle where others come down
column4: sledges are fast and hard to steer

column2: throwing snowballs
column3: only throw soft snowballs at people who are playing, never at faces, cars or strangers, and never put stones or ice in
column4: hard snowballs injure eyes and faces and can make drivers crash

column2: building a snow fort or tunnel
column3: keep it small and open and never dig tunnels in snow piles by the road
column4: snow can collapse and snowploughs push snow from the road

column2: icicles hanging from the roof
column3: do not stand under them or knock them down
column4: falling icicles are heavy and sharp

column2: walking on an icy pavement
column3: walk slowly with small steps, like a penguin, and keep your hands out of your pockets
column4: this keeps your balance and your hands free to catch a fall

column2: eating snow
column3: do not eat yellow, grey or dirty snow, and ask before eating any
column4: snow can contain dirt, animal pee and road salt

column2: a frozen puddle on the way to school
column3: walk around it or test with a toe while holding on to someone
column4: ice is slippery and can break into cold water

column2: snow sliding off a roof
column3: keep away from under roof edges after heavy snow
column4: heavy snow can slide down and bury or hurt someone

column2: going skiing or snowboarding
column3: wear a helmet, take lessons, and stay on marked runs
column4: falls and collisions on slopes are common and can be serious

column2: snow glare on a sunny winter day
column3: wear sunglasses or goggles and sunscreen
column4: sunlight reflected off snow can burn your skin and eyes

column2: ice skating on an outdoor rink
column3: skate in the same direction as others and get up quickly after a fall
column4: skate blades are sharp and can cut hands of people on the ice

column2: a car stuck in snow with its engine running
column3: tell the grown-up to make sure the exhaust pipe is clear of snow
column4: a blocked exhaust fills the car with carbon monoxide

column2: going out on a sunny day
column3: slip on a shirt, slop on sunscreen, slap on a hat, seek shade and slide on sunglasses
column4: strong sun burns skin, and sunburn in childhood raises the risk of skin cancer later

column2: a cloudy day in summer
column3: still wear sunscreen and a hat
column4: ultraviolet rays pass through clouds and burn skin

column2: the UV index is high
column3: stay in the shade in the middle of the day, about 11 a.m. to 3 p.m.
column4: the sun is strongest then, and in Australia and New Zealand it is especially strong

column2: looking straight at the sun
column3: never look directly at the sun, even with sunglasses
column4: it can permanently damage your eyes

column2: feeling hot, dizzy, with a headache and very thirsty
column3: move into the shade, drink water, cool down and tell a grown-up
column4: these are signs of heat exhaustion, which can turn into dangerous heatstroke

column2: a very hot day or heatwave
column3: drink water often, wear light clothes and play in the shade or indoors at the hottest time
column4: the body overheats quickly in strong heat

column2: a child or pet is left inside a parked car on a hot day
column3: tell a grown-up straight away so they can call for help
column4: a closed car heats up very fast and can kill within minutes

column2: getting sunburnt
column3: get out of the sun, cool the skin with cool water, drink, and tell a grown-up
column4: burnt skin needs care and more sun makes it worse

column2: a magnifying glass on a sunny day
column3: never point it at anything you could burn, at people or at animals
column4: it focuses sunlight into a spot hot enough to start fires

column2: a glass bottle lying in dry grass
column3: pick it up and take it to a bin
column4: a bottle can focus sunlight and start a grass fire

column2: a dog walk on a hot day
column3: feel the pavement with the back of your hand; if you cannot hold it there for five seconds it is too hot for paws
column4: hot pavements burn dogs' paws

column2: playing outside in light rain
column3: wear a raincoat and boots and change into dry clothes after
column4: wet clothes make you cold

column2: jumping in puddles
column3: jump only in shallow puddles away from roads and never in water you cannot see the bottom of
column4: deep or flooded puddles can hide holes, drains and sharp things

column2: walking on a wet day near the road
column3: walk away from the kerb
column4: cars splash and wet roads make it harder for cars to stop

column2: the myth that you catch a cold from being wet
column3: know that colds are caused by viruses, not rain, but still dry off and stay warm
column4: being cold and wet is unpleasant but germs cause colds

column2: water rushing along the gutters or drains
column3: keep away from storm drains, ditches and culverts
column4: fast water can sweep a child into a drain pipe

column2: floodwater across a road or path
column3: turn around, never walk, ride or drive through it
column4: just 15 cm of moving water can knock a person down and 30 cm can float a car

column2: a flood warning for your area
column3: listen to your grown-ups, move to higher ground if told to, and keep out of floodwater
column4: floodwater is fast, dirty and may hide holes and live electric cables

column2: playing in floodwater
column3: never play or swim in floodwater
column4: it contains sewage, chemicals and hidden dangers

column2: watching a rainbow
column3: stand with the sun behind you and look towards the rain
column4: a rainbow forms when sunlight bends in raindrops, and you cannot reach the end of it

column2: a long time with no rain and a drought
column3: save water: turn off the tap while brushing your teeth and take shorter showers
column4: water is precious and in a drought there may not be enough

column2: hearing thunder while playing outside
column3: go indoors at once: when thunder roars, go indoors
column4: if you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck by lightning

column2: no building nearby in a thunderstorm
column3: get into a hard-topped car, or crouch low away from tall trees, water and metal fences
column4: lightning hits tall objects and travels through water and metal

column2: sheltering under a tree in a thunderstorm
column3: never shelter under a lone tree
column4: lightning often strikes tall trees and the shock spreads to people under them

column2: swimming when a storm is coming
column3: get out of the water straight away
column4: water conducts electricity and swimmers are low in open water

column2: counting the seconds between lightning and thunder
column3: count the seconds and divide by three for kilometres (or by five for miles)
column4: sound travels slower than light, so the gap tells you how far away the storm is

column2: staying inside after the last thunder
column3: wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before going out again
column4: lightning can strike even when the storm seems to be moving away

column2: using a corded phone or a bath during a thunderstorm
column3: avoid baths, showers, washing up and corded phones until the storm passes
column4: lightning can travel through pipes and phone wires

column2: the myth that lightning never strikes twice in the same place
column3: know that lightning often strikes the same place, especially tall buildings
column4: tall places attract lightning again and again

column2: someone is struck by lightning
column3: call the emergency number at once; it is safe to touch them and help
column4: a person hit by lightning does not carry electricity and needs help fast

column2: big hailstones begin to fall
column3: go indoors and stay away from windows and skylights
column4: hail can hurt people and break glass

column2: a power cut during a storm
column3: use a torch, not candles, and keep the fridge closed
column4: candles start fires, and an open fridge loses its cold

column2: a fallen power line after a storm
column3: stay at least 10 metres (about 30 feet) away and tell a grown-up to call the power company
column4: a fallen line may still be live and can kill

column2: a tornado warning in the USA or Canada
column3: go to a basement or a small room without windows on the lowest floor, crouch down and cover your head
column4: most injuries come from flying debris and broken glass

column2: a tornado warning while in a mobile home or car
column3: go to a sturdy building or storm shelter
column4: mobile homes and cars can be thrown by a tornado

column2: a hurricane or cyclone is forecast
column3: help your family prepare: bring in loose garden things, pack an emergency kit and follow evacuation orders
column4: strong winds turn loose objects into missiles and storm surges flood coasts

column2: the eye of a hurricane passes and everything goes calm
column3: stay inside until the authorities say it is over
column4: the other side of the storm will come with strong winds again

column2: a severe weather warning on the radio, TV or phone
column3: listen to the warning and do what it says with your family
column4: warnings give time to get safe before the danger arrives

column2: a very windy day
column3: stay away from trees, scaffolding, fences and loose roof tiles
column4: wind can blow down branches and break loose objects

column2: playing on the beach in strong wind
column3: stay away from the edge of piers and harbour walls
column4: big waves and gusts can knock you into the sea

column2: riding a bike in strong side winds
column3: get off and walk, especially near traffic
column4: a gust can push you into the road

column2: walking to school in thick fog
column3: wear bright or reflective clothes, walk on the pavement and cross only at a crossing
column4: drivers cannot see you well in fog

column2: walking on hills or moors when fog comes in
column3: stop, stay together, and follow the path or wait with your grown-up
column4: in fog it is easy to lose your way and walk off a path or edge

column2: smelling smoke or seeing a bushfire or wildfire nearby
column3: tell a grown-up straight away and follow the family's fire plan
column4: fires move very fast, especially with wind

column2: a bushfire or wildfire evacuation order
column3: leave early with your family and do not go back for toys or pets in danger
column4: leaving early is the safest choice, and roads can become blocked

column2: the fire danger rating sign by the road says extreme
column3: know that no fires are allowed and your family should check plans
column4: in Australia, the USA and Canada these signs tell how dangerous fires would be

column2: smoky air from faraway fires
column3: stay indoors with windows closed and do not run around outside
column4: smoke harms the lungs, especially for people with asthma

column2: the ground starts shaking
column3: drop, cover under a sturdy table and hold on until the shaking stops
column4: most injuries come from falling objects and broken glass

column2: an earthquake while you are outside
column3: move away from buildings, trees, streetlights and power lines and drop to the ground
column4: falling bricks, glass and wires are the main dangers outdoors

column2: an earthquake while at the beach in New Zealand or on the Pacific coast
column3: if the shaking is long or strong, go to high ground or inland at once
column4: long or strong, get gone: a tsunami may follow within minutes

column2: needing the emergency number
column3: know your local number: 911 in the USA and Canada, 999 or 112 in the UK and Ireland, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand
column4: in an emergency there is no time to look it up

column2: a family emergency kit
column3: help pack water, food, a torch, batteries, a first aid kit and a radio
column4: in a storm or flood the power and shops may be closed for days

column2: the seasons in the northern and southern hemispheres
column3: know that when it is summer in the UK, USA and Canada, it is winter in Australia and New Zealand
column4: the Earth's tilt makes the hemispheres have opposite seasons

column2: autumn leaves on the pavement
column3: walk carefully on wet leaves
column4: wet leaves are as slippery as ice

column2: jumping into a pile of leaves
column3: check the pile first with a stick and never jump into a pile by the road
column4: piles can hide sticks, stones, hedgehogs, and cars may not see you

column2: spring is here and lambs are in the fields
column3: look but keep away from the lambs and keep dogs on a lead
column4: the mother sheep may panic and dogs can chase and hurt sheep

column2: pollen season and sneezing
column3: tell a grown-up if your eyes itch and you sneeze a lot outdoors
column4: it may be hay fever, an allergy that can be treated

column2: the days are short in winter
column3: wear bright or reflective clothes on the way home from school
column4: it gets dark early and drivers see you less

column2: the myth that the Earth is closer to the sun in summer
column3: know that seasons come from the tilt of the Earth, not its distance from the sun
column4: the northern summer happens when the Earth is actually a little further from the sun

column2: finding stinging nettles on the path
column3: keep away, and wear long trousers on overgrown paths
column4: tiny hairs on the leaves inject a liquid that stings and itches

column2: stung by nettles
column3: do not scratch; wash the skin with cool water and ask a grown-up for cream; a dock leaf may soothe it a little
column4: scratching spreads the itch, and the sting fades within a day

column2: leaves of three
column3: learn the rhyme «leaves of three, let it be» and avoid poison ivy and poison oak in North America
column4: their oil causes an itchy, blistering rash

column2: touching poison ivy
column3: wash the skin with soap and cool water as soon as possible and wash your clothes
column4: the oil stays on skin, clothes and pets and keeps spreading the rash

column2: burning poison ivy on a fire
column3: never burn it
column4: the smoke carries the oil into the lungs and is dangerous

column2: giant hogweed by a river
column3: never touch it; it is a very tall plant with huge white flower umbrellas
column4: its sap makes skin burn badly in sunlight

column2: blackberries on a hedge
column3: pick only berries a grown-up has identified, above dog height, away from roads, and wash them
column4: many berries look alike and some are poisonous

column2: red berries on a bush
column3: never eat wild berries, seeds or leaves unless a grown-up who knows plants says they are safe
column4: berries such as yew, holly, deadly nightshade and lords-and-ladies are poisonous

column2: a child has eaten an unknown berry or plant
column3: tell a grown-up at once and keep a sample of the plant; they will call poison control or a doctor
column4: quick help and knowing the plant help doctors treat poisoning

column2: finding mushrooms in the woods or lawn
column3: never pick and never eat wild mushrooms; wash your hands if you touched them
column4: some deadly mushrooms look like edible ones, and even experts make mistakes

column2: the myth that if an animal eats a plant it is safe
column3: know that animals can eat plants that are poisonous to people
column4: birds and squirrels eat berries that would make you sick

column2: sucking on a grass stem or flower
column3: do not put wild plants or flowers in your mouth
column4: some, such as foxgloves, daffodils and buttercups, are poisonous

column2: a thorny bush such as a rose or bramble
column3: move carefully and pull thorns out with a grown-up's help
column4: thorns scratch and can make cuts sore

column2: cacti in a dry garden or desert
column3: look but do not touch
column4: cactus spines go into skin and are hard to get out

column2: picking wild flowers
column3: leave wild flowers for others and for insects, and never pick protected ones
column4: many wild flowers are rare and some are protected by law

column2: a tree drops conkers, acorns or pine cones
column3: collect them for crafts but do not eat them
column4: conkers and acorns are poisonous to eat

column2: a wasp buzzing around your drink
column3: keep calm, cover drinks and use a straw, and check before you drink
column4: a wasp in a can can sting your mouth or throat

column2: stung by a bee
column3: tell a grown-up; scrape the sting out with a fingernail or card and put something cold on it
column4: scraping avoids squeezing more venom in; cold helps swelling

column2: someone's face or throat swells and they can't breathe after a sting
column3: call the emergency number at once and help them use their adrenaline auto-injector if they have one
column4: a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) can kill within minutes

column2: knocking down a wasps' nest
column3: never poke, throw stones at or touch a nest; tell a grown-up
column4: many wasps will come out to defend it and sting

column2: finding a tick on your skin after a walk
column3: tell a grown-up to remove it with fine tweezers close to the skin, pulling straight out
column4: ticks can carry Lyme disease, and quick removal lowers the risk

column2: coming home from long grass or woods
column3: check your body for ticks, especially behind the knees, armpits, hairline and ears
column4: ticks are tiny and like warm hidden places

column2: walking in long grass
column3: wear long trousers tucked into socks and use insect repellent with a grown-up's help
column4: this keeps ticks and biting insects off your skin

column2: mosquitoes in the evening
column3: cover your arms and legs and use repellent
column4: mosquito bites itch and in some places carry diseases

column2: scratching insect bites
column3: try not to scratch; use a cool cloth or anti-itch cream
column4: scratching can break the skin and cause infection

column2: seeing a snake on the path
column3: stop, back away slowly and give it space; never try to touch or catch it
column4: snakes only bite when they feel threatened, and some are venomous

column2: a snake bite
column3: keep still and calm, call the emergency number, and tell a grown-up; do not cut or suck the bite
column4: moving spreads the venom; in Australia a pressure bandage is used as first aid

column2: snakes in the UK and Ireland
column3: know that the adder is Britain's only venomous snake and Ireland has no wild snakes
column4: knowing local animals helps you stay calm and safe

column2: snakes in Australia and the USA
column3: stay on paths, wear boots, and never reach into holes, logs or long grass
column4: venomous snakes like brown snakes and rattlesnakes hide there

column2: a spider in your shoe or under an outdoor toilet seat in Australia
column3: shake out shoes and check seats before using them
column4: redback and funnel-web spiders hide in such places

column2: turning over a rock or log
column3: lift it towards you so the underside faces away from you, and put it back gently
column4: animals underneath can bite, and it is their home

column2: a caterpillar with long hairs
column3: look but do not touch
column4: the hairs of some caterpillars, such as the oak processionary, cause rashes

column2: an ant bite or fire ant nest
column3: keep away from ant hills and do not sit on them
column4: fire ants in parts of the USA and Australia sting many times

column2: bats in a cave or an injured bat
column3: never touch a bat; tell a grown-up
column4: bats can carry rabies, and a bite can be too small to notice

column2: a wild animal acting strangely or tame
column3: keep away and tell a grown-up
column4: it might be ill, perhaps with rabies

column2: finding a dead bird or animal
column3: do not touch it; tell a grown-up and wash your hands if you did
column4: dead animals can carry germs and parasites

column2: finding a needle or syringe on the ground
column3: never touch it; mark the spot and tell a grown-up
column4: needles can carry blood-borne diseases

column2: finding a bottle with liquid in it outdoors
column3: do not open, smell or drink from it
column4: it may contain chemicals or something dangerous

column2: finding money or a wallet outdoors
column3: give it to a grown-up so it can be handed to the police or the owner
column4: the owner will want it back

column2: finding a sharp rusty nail or metal
column3: do not pick it up with bare hands; tell a grown-up, and tell them if it cut you
column4: rusty cuts can cause tetanus infection

column2: finding animal poo on a path
column3: walk around it and never touch it
column4: it carries worms and germs

column2: finding fireworks, cartridges or flares on the ground
column3: never touch or pick them up; tell a grown-up
column4: they may still explode

column2: collecting stones, shells and leaves for school
column3: take only a few and only from places where it is allowed
column4: some parks and beaches forbid taking natural things

column2: finding a bird egg on the ground
column3: leave it where it is
column4: it may still have a living chick inside and it may be protected by law

column2: coming home from playing outside
column3: wash your hands with soap before eating
column4: outdoor dirt carries germs

column2: finishing a snack on a walk
column3: keep the wrapper in your pocket or bag until you find a bin
column4: litter harms animals and spoils places for everyone

column2: no bin in sight
column3: take your litter home
column4: «take only pictures, leave only footprints»

column2: finding litter that someone else dropped
column3: pick up safe litter with gloves or a litter picker and put it in a bin
column4: it helps animals and nature, and sets a good example

column2: throwing an apple core or banana peel into the bushes
column3: take it home or put it in a bin
column4: it takes months to rot, looks ugly and teaches animals to come close to people

column2: plastic rings from drinks cans
column3: cut them up before throwing away
column4: animals can get trapped in the rings

column2: letting go of a helium balloon
column3: never release balloons outdoors
column4: balloons come down as litter that animals swallow or get tangled in

column2: chewing gum on the ground
column3: wrap it in paper and put it in a bin
column4: gum is very hard to clean off and birds may eat it

column2: writing or painting on rocks in a park
column3: do not draw on rocks, trees or signs
column4: it spoils the place for others and is hard to remove

column2: building a stone tower or moving stones in a stream
column3: leave rocks where they are
column4: they are homes for insects and fish, and moving them damages the stream

column2: making a lot of noise in nature
column3: speak quietly and leave music at home
column4: noise frightens animals and disturbs other visitors

column2: taking home a frog, lizard or tadpole
column3: look but leave wild animals in their home
column4: they usually die in captivity and some are protected

column2: a sign in a national park or nature reserve
column3: read it and follow its rules
column4: reserves protect rare plants and animals

column2: walking with a dog in a nature reserve
column3: keep the dog on a lead and pick up its poo
column4: dogs chase wildlife and disturb ground-nesting birds

column2: seeing someone harm an animal or start a fire
column3: do not argue; tell a grown-up, a ranger or the police
column4: they can stop it safely

column2: finding an injured wild animal
column3: do not pick it up; tell a grown-up, who can call a wildlife rescue
column4: injured animals can bite and need expert care

column2: saving water outside
column3: turn off the hose when not using it and use a watering can
column4: clean water is limited, especially in dry summers

column2: looking at the stars on a clear night
column3: go somewhere dark away from street lights with a grown-up
column4: city lights hide the fainter stars

column2: finding the North Star
column3: follow the two end stars of the Big Dipper (the Plough) upwards
column4: the North Star shows the way north in the northern hemisphere

column2: looking for the North Star in Australia or New Zealand
column3: look for the Southern Cross instead
column4: the North Star cannot be seen from the southern hemisphere

column2: a shooting star
column3: know that it is a small piece of space rock burning up high in the air, not a star
column4: it heats up from rushing through the air

column2: the Moon changes shape
column3: know that the Moon does not change; we see different amounts of its sunlit side
column4: the Moon goes round the Earth once in about a month

column2: a solar eclipse
column3: never look at it without special eclipse glasses; ordinary sunglasses are not enough
column4: the sun can damage your eyes even when partly covered

column2: a lunar eclipse or a full moon
column3: you can look at the Moon safely with your eyes or binoculars
column4: moonlight is reflected sunlight and is not harmful

column2: the northern lights
column3: know they may be seen in Canada, Scotland and other far-north places, and the southern lights in New Zealand and Tasmania
column4: particles from the sun make the air glow near the poles

column2: being outside at night
column3: carry a torch, wear something bright and stay with a grown-up
column4: you can trip in the dark and drivers may not see you

column2: the myth that you should wait an hour after eating before swimming
column3: know that a snack is fine; but do not swim when very full or tired
column4: the old warning has no real evidence, but feeling unwell in water is still risky

column2: the myth that a bee dies every time it stings
column3: know that honeybees usually die after stinging people, but wasps and bumblebees do not
column4: a honeybee's barbed sting gets stuck in skin

column2: the myth that you can tell a mushroom is safe by how it looks or smells
column3: know that only an expert can tell, and you must never eat wild mushrooms
column4: deadly mushrooms can look, smell and taste nice

column2: the myth that rubbing snow on cold skin warms it
column3: know that rubbing harms frozen skin; warm it slowly instead
column4: rubbing damages frostbitten skin

column2: the myth that you should suck out snake venom
column3: know that sucking or cutting does not help and can harm
column4: the right help is keeping still and getting medical care

column2: the myth that rubber shoes protect you from lightning
column3: know that shoes give no protection; go indoors
column4: lightning is far too strong for a thin sole

column2: the myth that peeing on a jellyfish sting helps
column3: know that it does not help; follow local first aid
column4: urine can even make some stings worse

column2: the myth that a toad gives you warts
column3: know that touching a toad does not give warts, but wash your hands
column4: warts are caused by a human virus

column2: the myth that birds reject chicks touched by people
column3: know that most birds do not, but it is still best to leave chicks alone
column4: the parents are usually close and the chick is better with them
